h1: LMS vs YouTube and WhatsApp: free and blind, or structured and measured.
sub: Most coaching institutes start on YouTube and WhatsApp because both are free and every student already has them. This page sets out what that stack genuinely does well, what it cannot tell you, and the point at which a learning platform pays for itself.

sections.h2: Reach, or a record of who learned
paras: YouTube and WhatsApp are for a teacher who needs reach and conversation, quickly and at no cost. YouTube hosts video for any number of viewers and costs nothing. WhatsApp is where students already are, so announcements, doubts and material actually get seen. For a new institute, one subject and a small batch, this is the sensible start and there is no reason to rush past it.

A learning platform is for an institute that has to know something the free stack cannot tell it: who watched, who finished, who scored what, who has fallen behind, who has paid, and who is ready to be certified. The moment revenue depends on those answers, running blind becomes the expensive option.

body: Lessons are recorded or streamed on a video platform, material is shared as files in a group, tests are sent as PDFs and answers come back as photographs, doubts arrive between forwards and birthday messages, and fees are collected by transfer and ticked off in a spreadsheet. It works because every part is familiar, and because the teacher carries the structure in their head.

Three things are missing rather than broken. Progress: a view count is not a record of who watched what and how far they got. Assessment: a scanned answer sheet is not a score you can compare across a batch, and marking by hand limits how often you can test. Control: once a video and a PDF are shared they travel, and a group is a poor place to keep a paying cohort separate from a free one.

A learner mobile app holds the content library with video lessons, downloads and offline access, so students in low-connectivity areas can keep going. Quizzes and mock tests are auto-graded with instant scores and review, drawn from question banks. Batches and cohorts keep groups separate, with a timetable and recorded live classes. Progress runs per learner and per batch, so a student going quiet is visible before the parent calls. Certificates are issued on completion. Payments and fees are handled with GST, and WhatsApp reminders and Telegram bot nudges keep engagement where students already are.

sections.h2: Move when the answers start costing you
body: There is no virtue in buying a platform early. An institute with one batch, free content and a teacher who knows every student by name is well served by YouTube and WhatsApp. Keep the free stack while all three of these are true: you can name every student, you can remember who has paid, and nobody has asked you to prove a result.

ul: Move when you cannot answer a parent. The question is always the same: how is my child doing. If answering means scrolling a chat, the record is in the wrong place.
Move when marking limits testing. Institutes test less often than they should because marking is manual. Auto-graded mock tests change how often you can assess without changing your staffing.
Move when paid and free blur. Once a paying cohort exists, a shared link and an open group are a revenue leak. Batches keep the boundary without policing it.
Move when you certify. If completion has to be evidenced, certificates and compliance tracking are not optional. See certification platform.

body: Keep what works. The point of a platform is not to end the WhatsApp group, and the best setups still use it. What changes is that the content, the tests, the batch and the payment sit in a system that remembers, while the conversation stays where it always was. The approach came out of the founder's own government-exam-prep app on Google Play, which pairs an Android app with Telegram practice bots.

Before committing, run one batch through the platform alongside your existing groups for a term, and see how long it takes to answer three questions: who is behind, who has not paid, and who is ready to certify. See the Aura Learn demo or read coaching institute software.

sections.h2: LMS vs YouTube and WhatsApp, answered

items.q: Can a coaching institute run entirely on YouTube and WhatsApp?
items.a: Yes, and many do successfully at small scale. The limits are progress tracking, assessment at volume, access control between paid and free learners, and payment records. None matter with one small batch; all matter with several.

items.q: Do students have to stop using WhatsApp?
items.a: No. Aura Learn sends reminders and drip content over WhatsApp and nudges over a Telegram bot, because that is where students already are. The platform holds the course, the tests and the records; the conversation stays where it works.

items.q: What about students with poor internet?
items.a: Course video and material can be downloaded for offline access in the learner app, and progress syncs when the student is back in coverage. That matters more outside the metros than most feature lists admit.

items.q: Is an LMS priced per student?
items.a: Aura Learn is built for unlimited learners, so growing a batch does not change what you pay. The scope is agreed on a call rather than from a price list, because institutes differ in what they need switched on.

items.q: How do payments and fees work?
items.a: Payments, subscriptions and fees are handled in the platform with GST, so a learner's access, batch and payment status sit on the same record. That removes the spreadsheet that usually tracks who has paid.
